title: Seek vs scan
description: Understand index seeks and scans, when SQL Server chooses each, and how to influence the decision.

data.text: An index seek navigates the B-tree to a specific row or small range of rows. A scan reads all pages in an index or table from start to finish. In general, seeks are cheaper for small result sets and scans are cheaper when a large percentage of the table must be read anyway.

A seek is chosen when the predicate is highly selective and an appropriate index exists. The optimizer estimates the number of rows returned and compares the cost of seeking into the index and evaluating each row versus scanning the whole structure.

data.title: Query that typically produces a seek
data.content: Filtering by a unique or near-unique value on an indexed column usually produces a seek.

data.text: A scan is chosen when the result set is large relative to the table, no useful index exists, or the index is not selective enough. Scanning a nonclustered index and then looking up every row can be more expensive than scanning the clustered index once, especially when many columns are needed.

data.title: Query that may produce a scan
data.content: When filtering on a low-selectivity column like OrderStatus, the optimizer may choose a scan because too many rows match.

data.title: Seek is not always faster
data.text: If a query returns 90 percent of a 10-million-row table, an index seek followed by 9 million key lookups is far more expensive than a single clustered index scan. The optimizer is usually right about this.

data.title: Practical ways to influence the choice
items: Create indexes that match the WHERE clause and SELECT list
Update statistics so the optimizer has accurate row estimates
Use query hints only as a last resort; they can break as data changes
Consider filtered indexes for highly selective subsets of data

data.title: Takeaway
points: Seeks navigate the B-tree; scans read the whole structure
Selectivity is the main driver: high selectivity favors seeks
Scans are not always bad; they are often the cheapest option for large result sets
Statistics and index design are the proper tools to guide the optimizer
data.takeaway: Do not blindly prefer seeks over scans. Understand the row counts, selectivity, and index design behind the optimizer's choice.
